title: Crypto CTF Workflow
html:
Crypto CTF Workflow

Triage checklist

  1. Identify what you have: encoding vs encryption vs hash vs signature vs MAC.
  2. Determine what is controlled: plaintext/ciphertext, IV/nonce, key, oracle (padding/error/timing), partial leakage.
  3. Classify: symmetric (AES/CTR/GCM), public-key (RSA/ECC), hash/MAC (SHA/MD5/HMAC), classical (Vigenere/XOR).
  4. Apply the highest-probability checks first: decode layers, known-plaintext XOR, nonce reuse, mode misuse, oracle behavior.
  5. Escalate to advanced methods only when required: lattices (LLL/Coppersmith), SMT/Z3, side-channels.

Online resources & utilities

These are useful when the task is identification and layer peeling, or when you need quick confirmation of a hypothesis.

Hash lookups

  • Search for a challenge hash when it is known to be synthetic/public.
  • CrackStation.[1]
  • MD5Decrypt.[2]
  • hashes.org search.[3]
  • OnlineHashCrack.[4]
  • GPUHash.me.[5]
  • Hash Toolkit.[6]

Do not submit real password hashes or confidential challenge material to third-party lookup services. Prefer an offline wordlist/rule attack when disclosure, terms of service, or competition rules are a concern.

Identification helpers

  • CyberChef (Magic, decoding, and conversion).[7]
  • dCode (cipher/encoding playground).[8]
  • Boxentriq (substitution solvers).[9]

Practice platforms / references

  • CryptoHack (hands-on cryptography challenges).[10]
  • Cryptopals (classic modern-cryptography pitfalls).[11]

Automated decoding

  • Ciphey.[12]
  • python-codext (tries many bases/encodings).[13]

For esoteric-language source and custom interpreter state, see Crypto CTF Misc.

Encodings & classical ciphers

Technique

Many CTF crypto tasks are layered transforms: base encoding + simple substitution + compression. The goal is to identify layers and peel them safely.

Encodings: try many bases

If you suspect layered encoding (base64 → base32 → …), try:

  • CyberChef "Magic"
  • codext (python-codext): codext <string>

Common tells:

  • Base64: A-Za-z0-9+/= (padding = is common)
  • Base32: A-Z2-7= (often lots of = padding)
  • Ascii85/Base85: dense punctuation; sometimes wrapped in <~ ~>

Substitution / monoalphabetic

  • Boxentriq cryptogram solver.[9]
  • quipqiup.[14]

Known-plaintext recovery of substituted Base32 filenames

When an obfuscated filename uses only a-z2-7, expands to about ceil(8 * byte_length / 5) characters after a fixed suffix is removed, and the same plaintext produces the same output across files, test unpadded Base32 followed by a fixed symbol substitution. These clues are not proof by themselves. Collect predictable filenames and their ciphertexts, preserve case, Base32-encode each plaintext, and align symbols position by position. Every repeated plaintext symbol must map to the same ciphertext symbol, and the inverse mapping must also be unique. In one ransomware case, ntuser.ini and NTUSER.DAT provided such pairs; this recovered filenames, not file contents or encryption keys.[28]

import base64
pairs = [("ntuser.ini", "zsub5mdlekr37dx4"), ("NTUSER.DAT", "4s5l5tul5kr6kv5t")]
forward, inverse = {}, {}
for name, ciphertext in pairs:
    b32 = base64.b32encode(name.encode("ascii")).decode().lower().rstrip("=")
    assert len(b32) == len(ciphertext)
    for p, c in zip(b32, ciphertext):
        assert forward.get(p, c) == c and inverse.get(c, p) == p
        forward[p], inverse[c] = c, p
target = "4s5l5tul5kr6kv5t"  # Remove the fixed suffix first
b32 = "".join(inverse[c] for c in target)
clear = base64.b32decode(b32.upper() + "=" * (-len(b32) % 8))
assert "".join(forward[c] for c in b32) == target
print(clear.decode("ascii"))

If a target contains unmapped symbols, obtain more known pairs or permute only the unused Base32-symbol mappings. Restore padding to an eight-character boundary, reject invalid Base32 and non-printable decoded names, then re-encode surviving candidates and compare the entire original ciphertext. Repeated ciphertext blocks can supply additional guesses: in the case above, 3gpng2wv mapped back to Base32 gaydambq, which decodes to five ASCII zeroes. A printable candidate alone is not a unique proof.[28]

Caesar / ROT / Atbash

  • Nayuki automatic Caesar-cipher breaker.[15]
  • Rumkin Atbash tool.[16]

Vigenère

  • dCode Vigenère tool.[8]
  • Guballa Vigenère solver.[17]

Bacon cipher

Often appears as groups of 5 bits or 5 letters:

00111 01101 01010 00000 ...
AABBB ABBAB ABABA AAAAA ...

Morse

.... --- .-.. -.-. .- .-. .- -.-. --- .-.. .-

Runes

Runes are frequently substitution alphabets; search for "futhark cipher" and try mapping tables.

Compression in challenges

Technique

Compression shows up constantly as an extra layer (zlib/deflate/gzip/xz/zstd), sometimes nested. If output almost parses but looks like garbage, suspect compression.

Quick identification

  • file <blob>
  • Look for magic bytes:
  • gzip: 1f 8b
  • zlib: commonly 78 01, 78 5e, 78 9c, or 78 da (the second byte depends on compression flags)
  • zip: 50 4b 03 04
  • bzip2: 42 5a 68 (BZh)
  • xz: fd 37 7a 58 5a 00
  • zstd: 28 b5 2f fd

Raw DEFLATE

CyberChef has Raw Deflate/Raw Inflate, which is often the fastest path when the blob looks compressed but zlib fails.

Useful CLI

python3 - blob.bin <<'PY'
import sys, zlib
data = open(sys.argv[1], 'rb').read()
for wbits in [zlib.MAX_WBITS, -zlib.MAX_WBITS]:
  try:
    print(zlib.decompress(data, wbits=wbits)[:200])
  except Exception:
    <PASSWORD>
PY

Common CTF crypto constructs

Technique

These appear frequently because they are realistic developer mistakes or common libraries used incorrectly. The goal is usually recognition and applying a known extraction or reconstruction workflow.

Fernet

Typical hint: two Base64 strings (token + key).

  • Decoder/notes: Asecuritysite Fernet decoder.[18]
  • In Python: from cryptography.fernet import Fernet

Shamir Secret Sharing

If you see multiple shares and a threshold t is mentioned, it is likely Shamir.

  • Online reconstructor (for non-sensitive CTF shares only).[19]

OpenSSL salted formats

CTFs sometimes give openssl enc outputs (header often begins with Salted__).

Bruteforce helpers:

  • bruteforce-salted-openssl.[20]
  • easy_BFopensslCTF.[21]

General toolset

  • RsaCtfTool.[22]
  • featherduster.[23]
  • cryptovenom.[24]

Recommended local setup

Practical CTF stack:

  • Python plus pycryptodome for symmetric primitives and fast prototyping.[25]
  • SageMath for modular arithmetic, CRT, lattices, and RSA/ECC work.[26]
  • Z3 for constraint-based challenges (when the crypto reduces to constraints).[27]

Suggested Python packages:

pip install pycryptodome gmpy2 sympy pwntools z3-solver
